title: US breeding birds on 2,985 survey routes followed only 10-40% of their spatial land-cover gradients when land cover changed in 1985-2025; land-cover change did not cause the weak temperature tracking
abstract: Question: bird community temperature indices (CTI) of the North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) follow only a small part of their spatial temperature slope in time. Did land-cover change hide part of the climate response? And do birds follow their spatial land-cover gradients in time at full strength, so that weak tracking is specific to climate? Data: BBS 2026 release, 75,846 standard runs on 2,985 contiguous-US routes, 1985-2025; Annual NLCD Collection 1.2 land cover for nine map years in 400 m, 1 km and 3 km buffers around route paths; nClimGrid climate; AVONET habitat guilds. Method (plan written before outcomes): spatial models of base-period (1985-1994) CTI, guild shares and 359 species' counts on land-cover shares at fixed climate and region; temporal tests with route x observer and year effects (1 = full space-for-time transfer); cross-fitting, lead placebo, lags; 2-degree block bootstrap. Results: near the routes, crops fell 2.3 percentage points, evergreen forest 1.1, and developed land rose 2.6. At fixed climate, land cover explained 37% of the remaining spatial CTI variation. In time, the CTI followed 0.17 (95% CI 0.05-0.28) of its habitat-predicted change. Guild shares followed 0.14-0.43 (forest 0.22, grassland 0.14, shrub 0.43); in matched single-habitat tests the human-modified guild followed 0.00 (-0.44 to 0.61) and only wetland birds followed water change fully (1.8, 1.0-2.6). Species followed a mean 0.21 (SE 0.04) of their own cross-fitted habitat gradients (wetland 0.53, forest 0.15, shrub 0.08). Future land cover gave no signal (-0.08, SE 0.05), lags added little, and 1 km or 3 km buffers, smoothed land cover and flip-noise reliability (0.82-1.00) did not change the deficit. Land-cover change predicted a CTI trend of +0.0046 C per decade with full transfer of community coefficients (13% of the observed 0.035) and +0.0001 to +0.0008 with realized or species-based transfer, always zero or toward warm species, against a warming-expected 0.099. Conclusion: land-use change does not cancel the climate signal in BBS communities; weak space-for-time transfer also holds for directly measured habitat, so spatial gradients overstate decadal responses to slow drivers in general. Limitations: modelled land cover, possible non-habitat confounding of spatial slopes, 1966-1998 route paths, reduced bootstrap draws on a loaded host.

display.caption: A: mean change of land-cover shares within 400 m of 2,985 BBS route paths, 1985-2024 (Annual NLCD). B: species temporal response to their own cross-fitted spatial land-cover gradient (gamma), mean and 95% CI by AVONET guild; 1 = full space-for-time transfer. Blue band: range of temperature transfer in earlier campaign work (0.03-0.24).

Community indices: temporal slope divided by spatial slope for matched guild-habitat pairs (400 m buffer, smoothed land-cover path, 3 km buffer) and for the CTI on its habitat-predicted value. 2-degree block-bootstrap 95% intervals. Only wetland birds follow water change fully.

CTI trends 1985-2025 (route x observer effects): observed, warming-expected (spatial slope x warming), and five estimates of the land-cover contribution. All land-cover estimates are near zero or positive.
